steps.text:
Welcome back, [b]General[/b]. This time you command [b]Germany[/b].

Last lesson you watched Status and Response cards. Today you play them.

Two [b]Status[/b] cards are already face up on your table, played on earlier turns.

Each cost a whole Play step once. They have worked for free ever since, and will every turn until the war ends.
[b]Bias for Action[/b]: [i]Use once per turn when you build an Army. Discard the top 1 card of your draw deck to battle a land space adjacent to the Army just built.[/i]
[b]Blitzkrieg[/b]: [i]Use once per turn when you battle a land space. Discard the top 1 card of your draw deck to build an Army in the space battled.[/i]

Read them together. A build sets off a battle, and the battle sets off another build.

That is a [b]chain[/b], General. One card from your hand can set off all of it.
Your [b]Play[/b] step. Play [b]Build Army[/b]. The rest of your hand is greyed out for now.

Build in [b]Eastern Europe[/b].

It scores nothing. But it touches [b]Ukraine[/b], where a Soviet army stands on a supply star.

You built an Army, so [b]Bias for Action[/b] is offering itself.

The game asks every time a card on your table could be used. You never have to say yes.

This time, [b]use it[/b].

The price is on the card: the top card of your draw deck goes to the discard pile, sight unseen.

Bias for Action lets you battle a land space next to the Army you just built.

Battle the Soviet army in [b]Ukraine[/b].

The chain carries on. You battled a land space, so [b]Blitzkrieg[/b] is offering itself.

Use it: one more card off your deck, and an Army moves into Ukraine.

Count what one card bought, General: an army in Eastern Europe, a Soviet army destroyed, and Ukraine's supply star.

The price was two cards off your draw deck. Cheap, but not free. The deck never refills.

Mind the words [b]once per turn[/b].

Blitzkrieg's army was a [i]build[/i] too, so it could have set off Bias for Action again. But Bias for Action was already spent this turn.
[b]The United Kingdom[/b]. Watch where their army appears.

A British army in [b]Australia[/b], half a world from the nearest British unit.

[b]Increased Commonwealth Support[/b] did not [i]build[/i] that army. It [b]recruited[/b] it.

To [b]build[/b], you need a supplied unit of your own next to the space, unless it is your home space.

To [b]recruit[/b], you place the unit where the card says. Nothing needs to be next to it.

Two catches. A recruited unit still needs [b]supply[/b]. Australia has a supply star, so it feeds itself.

And a recruit is [b]not a build[/b]. "When you build" cards, like Bias for Action, never fire on one.
[b]Japan[/b]. Your ally has a Response card face down on its table. Watch what sets it off.

Japan built a navy in the [b]Sea of Japan[/b], and its Response wakes up.

[b]Special Naval Landing Forces[/b]: [i]Use when you build a Navy. Build two Armies adjacent to the space where you built the Navy.[/i]

One card, three units: a navy, and armies in [b]Vladivostok[/b] and [b]Iwo Jima[/b].

No enemy did anything. Japan set off its [b]own[/b] Response. A trigger does not have to come from the enemy.

And now that Response is discarded. One use, then gone.

Your Status cards stay on the table and fire again next turn.
[b]The Soviet Union[/b]. You took Ukraine from them. They will not let that stand.

[b]General Winter[/b]: [i]Eliminate 1 or 2 Axis Armies in or adjacent to Moscow.[/i]

Your army in Ukraine is gone. No battle, just an Event card, used once and discarded.

Eastern Europe is not next to Moscow, so that army still stands.

Your Status cards are face up. The Soviets could read them, and knew where your armies would end up.
[b]Italy[/b], your other ally. They already hold the [b]Mediterranean Sea[/b].

Italy has built an army in [b]North Africa[/b]. No supply star there. So why bother?

Because North Africa is a [b]strait[/b].

A [b]strait[/b] is a land space that controls the water beside it. North Africa sits between the [b]North Sea[/b] and the [b]Mediterranean[/b].

For the team that does [i]not[/i] hold it, those two seas stop being adjacent.

So the Allies can no longer build, battle or trace supply between those two seas.

Mind one detail: an [b]empty[/b] strait belongs to the [b]Allies[/b]. The Axis must stand on it to close it.

The map has five: [b]North Africa[/b], the [b]Middle East[/b], [b]Scandinavia[/b], [b]South East Asia[/b] and [b]Latin America[/b].

One army, no points, and the Royal Navy's road into the Mediterranean is shut.

[b]The United States[/b] wants [b]US West[/b], a supply star next door.

The trouble is their hand: not one Build Army card in it.

[b]Reallocate Resources[/b] is beside every faction's hand, every turn.

Instead of playing a card, discard [b]4 cards[/b]. Then take a Build or Battle card from your draw deck and play it at once.

An army in [b]US West[/b], from a hand that could not build one.

But it cost five cards instead of one: four from the hand, and the Build Army from the deck. Use it when the card you need is the one you do not hold.

The Americans soften the blow with [b]Rosie the Riveter[/b], already on their table:

[i]Use once per turn at the beginning of your Discard step. Take 1 or 2 cards from your hand and place them on the bottom of your draw deck.[/i]

A useless card goes [b]under[/b] the deck instead of into the discard pile. It comes back late in the war, when a dry deck would cost points.

That is a good Status card: a small edge, every turn.
One round, and you have seen chained Status cards, a self-triggered Response, an Event, a recruit, a strait and Reallocate Resources.

One round left, and your hand is your own.

There is a [b]Land Battle[/b] in it, and Blitzkrieg is still on your table.

The card you play is only half your turn, General. The other half is already on the table: yours face up, theirs face down.

[b]Dismissed.[/b]
